what: First Majestic Silver mines silver and gold. It operates mines in Mexico and the United States, processes the ore into concentrate and bullion, and owns a mint that sells silver coins and bars directly to retail buyers. Silver is its primary metal, which makes it unusual among precious metals miners.
customers: Metal traders, smelters and refiners who buy its concentrate and bullion, plus retail investors who buy coins and bars directly from its mint.
money: Silver produced from its Mexican and American mines, sold as concentrate, doré and bullion.
Gold produced alongside silver, which has become a larger share of revenue.
Direct retail sales of coins and bars.
moat: A producing silver mine is a scarce asset: most silver comes as a by-product of copper and lead mining, so companies whose primary metal is silver are few. Owning permitted, operating mines with known reserves in Mexico cannot be replicated quickly, because permitting and community agreements take years. The mint is a small but unusual advantage, selling at retail prices rather than wholesale.
risks: Revenue leapt from $560.6M in 2024 to $1.3B in 2025, driven substantially by metal prices rather than production — which means it can reverse the same way.
Mining in Mexico carries real political and operational risk: tax disputes, community relations, security problems and changing mining law have all affected the company.
Only two analysts cover the stock, so the $23.75 average target against an $11.34 price rests on almost no coverage.
Silver is more volatile than gold because roughly half its demand is industrial, so it falls with manufacturing as well as with precious metals sentiment.
Operating costs at individual mines have historically been higher than planned, and a mine that cannot produce below the metal price has no value.
opportunities: A net margin of 13.1% and free cash flow of $571.3M on $1.8B of revenue, with the shares at about 9.8 times free cash flow and 4.6 times EV/EBITDA.
Cash of $793.4M against $292.2M of debt is a strong net cash position for a miner.
Silver has both industrial demand — notably solar panels and electronics — and investment demand, which gives it two separate sources of support.
Gold has become a substantial part of production, which diversifies the revenue away from silver’s volatility.
Operating leverage is enormous: at a fixed cost base, every dollar of metal price increase goes almost entirely to profit.
watch: All-in sustaining cost per silver equivalent ounce, and production volumes. The metal price is not something the company controls; cost per ounce is the only thing that is, and it decides whether high prices become profit.
view: Mining companies are leveraged bets on metal prices wearing the costume of operating businesses, and First Majestic’s recent numbers make the point better than any argument could. Revenue went from $561 million in 2024 to $1.3 billion in 2025. Production did not double. Metal prices rose, and because the cost base is largely fixed, almost all of that increase landed in profit. That operating leverage is the entire attraction, and it works identically in reverse.

The asset is genuinely scarce in a way that is often overlooked. Most of the world’s silver arrives as a by-product of mining copper, lead and zinc, which means silver supply does not respond to the silver price — it responds to base metal demand. Companies whose primary metal is silver are consequently few, and permitted, operating mines with known reserves cannot be created quickly: permitting, community agreements and construction take years. The mint is a small oddity worth noting, selling coins at retail prices rather than concentrate at wholesale.

Silver’s demand profile is the part to think carefully about. Roughly half of it is industrial — solar panels most prominently, plus electronics — and half is investment. That gives two sources of support in good times and two sources of weakness in bad ones: silver falls when manufacturing weakens and when precious metals sentiment turns, which is why it is consistently more volatile than gold. The growing gold share of production usefully dampens this.

The risk that has actually cost shareholders money here is Mexico rather than metal prices: tax disputes, changing mining law, community relations and security problems have all hit this company in the past, and none of them is resolved permanently. At 4.6 times EV/EBITDA with $793 million of cash against $292 million of debt, the balance sheet can survive a downturn, which is more than many miners can say. All-in sustaining cost per ounce is the only number management controls, and it is the one that decides whether a high metal price becomes profit or disappears into the mine.
bull: Silver and gold prices hold, enormous operating leverage on a fixed cost base converts them straight to profit, and a net-cash balance sheet funds it all.
bear: Metal prices fall and the leverage reverses, while Mexican tax, legal and security problems raise costs per ounce at the same time.
